structs.name: CSWSCreature
structs.how_to_obtain: g_pAppManager (global at 0x007A39FC) -> +8 CServerExoApp* -> CServerExoApp::GetCreatureByGameObjectID(0x4AE770, id). That thunk does `mov ecx,[ecx+4]` then jumps to CServerExoAppInternal::GetCreatureByGameObjectID (0x4B1790), which looks the id up in the object array, checks the type byte at obj+8 == 5, and calls vtable+0x30. Slot 0x30 on the creature vtable (0x7470C8) is `mov eax,ecx; ret`, so the returned CSWSCreature* is bit-identical to the CGameObject* -- no pointer adjustment.

fields.name: field_324
fields.meaning: area-of-effect object ids; data ptr at 0x324, size at 0x328, u32 elements

fields.name: field_330
fields.meaning: object id list; data ptr at 0x330, size at 0x334, u32 elements

fields.name: creature_stats
fields.meaning: CSWSCreatureStats* - all ability scores, feats, class levels live behind this pointer

structs.name: CSWCCreature
structs.how_to_obtain: Two ways. Cheap: get the CSWSCreature first, then read CSWSObject+548 (client_object) -- CSWSObject::GetClientObject 0x4CC2B0 does exactly that. Independent: g_pAppManager (0x007A39FC) -> +4 CClientExoApp* -> CClientExoApp::GetCreatureByGameObjectID (0x5ED5B0), which forwards to CClientExoAppInternal::GetCreatureByGameObjectID (0x5F1180).

fields.name: moving_orientation
fields.meaning: SetMovingOrientation 0x60B380 copies 3 dwords here from a Vector*

fields.name: field_1dc
fields.meaning: flds 0x1dc/0x1e0/0x1e4 subtracted from position at 0x24/0x28/0x2c -- a destination point, NOT an array list

structs.name: CSWSCreatureStats
structs.how_to_obtain: CSWSCreature + 2676 (creature_stats pointer). Not reachable directly from the object array; you must have the creature first. The back-pointer at CSWSCreatureStats+36 returns to the owning CSWSCreature.

fields.name: feats
fields.meaning: feat list; data ptr at 0, size at 4, capacity at 8. Elements are u16 feat ids

fields.name: race
fields.meaning: race id. Two bytes, NOT the int Ghidra emits -- the next field is named field_de, which pins it

fields.name: portrait
fields.meaning: portrait resref; note this is at an odd offset (0x16e), not dword-aligned

structs.name: CSWSObject
structs.how_to_obtain: g_pAppManager (0x007A39FC) -> +8 CServerExoApp* -> CServerExoApp::GetGameObject(0x4AE750, id) returns a CGameObject*. Every server-side subclass embeds CSWSObject at a known offset (creature/placeable/door/trigger at 0, item at 16), so once the type byte tells you which subclass it is, the CSWSObject sits at that fixed offset from the returned pointer.

fields.name: game_object
fields.meaning: embedded base object: vtable, id, type byte

fields.name: position
fields.meaning: world position x,y,z -- flds 0x90/0x94/0x98 throughout CSWSObject. This is the field a Phasor-style script would call readfloat(base+0xF8) for

fields.name: orientation
fields.meaning: facing vector; CSWSObject::SetOrientation 0x4CD170 copies exactly 3 dwords here from a Vector*

fields.name: effects
fields.meaning: applied CGameEffect* list. data ptr at 0x124, size at 0x128, capacity at 0x12c

fields.name: field_1fc
fields.meaning: dirty/update flag word: SetOrientation ORs bit 2 into it

fields.name: client_object
fields.meaning: CSWCObject* client half; CSWSObject::GetClientObject 0x4CC2B0 reads and caches this slot

structs.name: CSWCObject
structs.how_to_obtain: CSWSObject + 548 (client_object), or g_pAppManager -> +4 CClientExoApp* -> CClientExoApp::GetGameObject (0x5ED580). The back-link is CSWCObject+248, read by CSWCObject::GetServerObject 0x63D4B0.

fields.name: orientation
fields.meaning: client facing; CSWCObject::SetOrientation 0x63C110 copies 3 dwords here

fields.name: server_object
fields.meaning: CSWSObject* server half; CSWCObject::GetServerObject 0x63D4B0 reads and caches this slot

structs.name: CGameObject
structs.how_to_obtain: CGameObjectArray::GetGameObject (0x4D8230) writes one of these into its out-parameter. Every game object begins with this header, so the pointer you get from the id lookup IS a CGameObject*.

fields.name: vtable
fields.meaning: vtable. Slots 0x18/0x30/0x38/0x50/0x58/0x5c/0x64/0x68 are type-checked downcasts: on the matching class the slot is `mov eax,ecx; ret`, otherwise `xor eax,eax; ret`

fields.name: id
fields.meaning: object id. Bit 31 selects one of two id spaces; the low 12 bits are the hash bucket

fields.name: object_type
fields.meaning: object type, ONE byte (Ghidra emits `int` here and that is wrong). Verified: 4=area 5=creature 6=item 7=trigger 9=placeable 10=door 11=area-of-effect 12=waypoint 13=encounter 16=sound. Byte compare at 0x4B17BE and 0x4CC114

structs.name: CSWSArea
structs.how_to_obtain: g_pAppManager -> +8 CServerExoApp* -> CServerExoApp::GetAreaByGameObjectID (0x4AE780). Or from any object: read CSWSObject+140 (area_id) and look that id up the same way. Note the embedded CGameObject is at +284, not +0.

fields.name: sw_area
fields.meaning: 256-byte area header ahead of the embedded CGameObject

fields.name: game_objects
fields.meaning: CExoArrayList.data - u32 object ids of everything in the area. Ghidra split this list into three scalar fields instead of one blob (CSWSArea::AddObjectToArea 0x50DFD0)

fields.name: field_1a0
fields.meaning: CExoArrayList.data - grown through CExoArrayList::Allocate 0x5E03C0 from CSWSDoor::AddToArea. Another split-form list

structs.name: CSWSModule
structs.how_to_obtain: g_pAppManager (0x007A39FC) -> +8 CServerExoApp* -> CServerExoApp::GetModule (0x4AE6B0). That thunk hops to CServerExoAppInternal::GetModule (0x4B14F0), which reads the module object id at CServerExoAppInternal+0x10060 and resolves it through the same object array. Only one module is live at a time.

fields.name: object_lookup_table
fields.meaning: object lookup table; data ptr at 0x130, size at 0x134, elements are 40 (0x28) bytes each

fields.name: area
fields.meaning: CSWSArea* of the currently loaded area

structs.name: CSWSPlaceable
structs.how_to_obtain: g_pAppManager -> +8 CServerExoApp* -> CServerExoApp::GetPlaceableByGameObjectID (0x4AE7A0). Internal at 0x4B18D0 checks the type byte == 9 and calls vtable+0x58.

structs.name: CSWSDoor
structs.how_to_obtain: g_pAppManager -> +8 CServerExoApp* -> CServerExoApp::GetDoorByGameObjectID (0x4AE7C0). Internal at 0x4B1920 checks the type byte == 10 and calls vtable+0x18, which on the door vtable (0x7498B0) is `mov eax,ecx; ret`.

fields.name: bounding_box_1
fields.meaning: bounding box corner, passed as a Vector* in CSWSDoor::AddToArea 0x58B6D0

structs.name: CSWSTrigger
structs.how_to_obtain: g_pAppManager -> +8 CServerExoApp* -> CServerExoApp::GetTriggerByGameObjectID (0x4AE790). Internal at 0x4B1880 checks the type byte == 7.

structs.name: CSWSItem
structs.how_to_obtain: g_pAppManager -> +8 CServerExoApp* -> CServerExoApp::GetItemByGameObjectID (0x4AE760). Internal at 0x4B1740 checks the type byte == 6 and calls vtable+0x38. Careful: the embedded CSWSObject starts at +16, not +0, so the raw CGameObject* is at item+16, not item+0.

fields.name: item
fields.meaning: 16-byte item header ahead of the embedded CSWSObject

fields.name: item_repo
fields.meaning: CItemRepository* that currently holds this item

structs.name: CItemRepository
structs.how_to_obtain: CSWSCreature+2608 (item_repo), CSWSPlaceable+876 (item_repository), or CSWPartyTable+280 (pt_item_repo). Items name their owning repository at CSWSItem+620.

fields.name: items_list
fields.meaning: element storage of an inlined CExoArrayList: data at 12, size at 16, capacity at 20

structs.name: CExoString
structs.how_to_obtain: Always inline in a parent struct. Never heap-allocated on its own in these layouts.

fields.name: c_string
fields.meaning: char* buffer; may be NULL for an empty string

fields.name: length
fields.meaning: byte length, not including the terminator

structs.name: CExoArrayList
structs.how_to_obtain: Always inline in a parent struct. This is the single most important 12 bytes in the whole set -- see access_notes.

fields.name: data
fields.meaning: element storage. Reading this slot as an int gives you a POINTER, not element 0. operator[] at 0x437C40 is `mov eax,[ecx]; lea eax,[eax+i*elemsize]`

fields.name: size
fields.meaning: live element count. CExoArrayList::Add increments this slot (`incl 0x4(%esi)` at 0x42141F). Iterate 0 .. size-1

fields.name: capacity
fields.meaning: allocated slots. Add compares size against this and doubles (min 8) when they are equal. Never iterate to capacity

structs.name: CExoLinkedList
structs.how_to_obtain: Inline in a parent struct. Ghidra recovered no interior structure -- it is four opaque bytes, almost certainly a single head pointer.

structs.name: CScriptEvent
structs.how_to_obtain: Handed to script-event handlers by the engine; not looked up by id. THIS IS THE STRUCT THE PROJECT ALREADY GOT WRONG ONCE.

fields.name: int_params
fields.meaning: NOT an int array. 0x4 = data pointer, 0x8 = size, 0xc = capacity. The ints live at *(int**)(ev+4)

fields.name: string_params
fields.meaning: 0x1c = data pointer (to CExoString elements), 0x20 = size, 0x24 = capacity

fields.name: object_params
fields.meaning: 0x28 = data pointer (to u32 object ids), 0x2c = size, 0x30 = capacity

structs.name: CVirtualMachine
structs.how_to_obtain: A 4-byte wrapper holding one pointer. All 22 public methods (RunScript 0x5D0FC0, StackPopInteger 0x5D1000, StackPushObject 0x5D10D0, ...) are thin forwarders onto the internal.

structs.name: CVirtualMachineInternal
structs.how_to_obtain: CVirtualMachine+0. The CVirtualMachine itself is a process global reached from the VM entry points, not from CAppManager.

structs.name: CServerExoApp
structs.how_to_obtain: *(CAppManager**)0x007A39FC then +8. Every server-side object getter hangs off this.

fields.name: internal
fields.meaning: CServerExoAppInternal*. Every public getter starts `mov ecx,[ecx+4]` and jumps to the internal method

structs.name: CAppManager
structs.how_to_obtain: *(CAppManager**)0x007A39FC. This one global is the root of everything. 5680 instructions in the image reference it.

fields.name: buffer
fields.meaning: large temp buffer, allocated lazily by CAppManager::AllocLargeTempBuffer 0x4010A0

fields.name: server
fields.meaning: CServerExoApp*. This is the hop every server lookup makes: `mov ecx,[g_pAppManager]; mov ecx,[ecx+8]`

structs.name: CGameObjectArray
structs.how_to_obtain: CServerExoAppInternal + 0x1005C. Client side: CClientExoApp::GetGameObjectArray 0x5ED570.

fields.name: object_tree
fields.meaning: hash table, NOT a tree despite the name. 8192 dword buckets. bucket index = ((id>>31)&1)*0x1000 + (id & 0xFFF). Each chain node is 12 bytes {u32 id_masked, void* object, node* next} (CGameObjectArray::GetGameObject 0x4D8230)

structs.name: CSWPartyTable
structs.how_to_obtain: g_pAppManager -> +8 CServerExoApp* -> CServerExoApp::GetPartyTable (0x4AEE70).

structs.name: CGameEffect
structs.how_to_obtain: Elements of the CExoArrayList at CSWSObject+292 (effects). Read the data pointer at +292, the count at +296, then index CGameEffect* elements.

fields.name: type
fields.meaning: effect type. TWO bytes -- `movzwl 0x8(%ecx),%edx` at 0x503A70 proves it. Ghidra emits `int` here, which shifts every later field by 2 and makes the whole struct wrong

fields.name: num_integers
fields.meaning: SetNumIntegers 0x503630 writes 0x30 then reallocates the array at 0x34

fields.name: integer_list
fields.meaning: heap int array of num_integers entries. GetInteger 0x503690: `mov eax,[ecx+0x34]; mov eax,[eax+i*4]`

fields.name: string_list
fields.meaning: inline array of six 8-byte CExoStrings. CopyStringFromList 0x503700: `lea ecx,[ecx+i*8+0x48]`

fields.name: object_list
fields.meaning: inline array of four object ids. GetObjectID 0x5036E0: `mov eax,[ecx+i*4+0x78]`

structs.name: C2DA
structs.how_to_obtain: Owned by the resource manager, not by the object array. Not reachable from CAppManager in these layouts -- you need a 2DA cache lookup by name.

access_notes:
SOURCE AND HOW TO RE-DERIVE

Corpus: `python3 tools/kpdiscover.py --corpus` gives the sqlite path. All 25 definitions come from `ghidra_type` at `binary_id=8` (K1 Windows GOG swkotor.exe, md5 9a44891011437deb6536d992bccdfe4b, image base 0x400000). Every disassembly claim below was checked against the matching raw image in the corpus `extract/raw` tree with `i686-w64-mingw32-objdump -d --start-address= --stop-address=`, addresses are absolute VAs. binary_id 5 and 19 carry the same type names with zero fields, so binary_id=8 is the only rich K1 source.

DURABLE ARTIFACT (repo-relative, promote if wanted): `tmp/structwork/k1_structs.json` (full), `tmp/structwork/k1_structs_slim.json` (what is reproduced above), `tmp/structwork/listing.txt` (flat), `tmp/structwork/oracle.py` (the verifier).

TYPE SHORTHAND: ptr=32-bit pointer, u8/u16/u32/u64 unsigned, i8/i16/i32 signed, f32 float. `T[0xN]` is an inline array of N elements. CExoArrayList/Vector/CExoString/CExoLocString/CResRef/CScriptVarTable/CGameObject/CSWSObject/CSWCObject are the named structs, embedded inline.

CONFIDENCE: absent = high (Ghidra field plus, where noted, a disassembly check). `med` = the name is Ghidra's and the type is inferred from size plus naming. `low` = shape unknown. A field named `field_<hex>` or `_pad<hex>` is a Ghidra placeholder: the offset and width are exact, the meaning was never recovered. Treat all of those as low-confidence in meaning. Where a placeholder-named field carries a type or meaning claim from me, an explicit confidence is attached.

HOW THE LAYOUTS WERE VERIFIED (this matters, totals alone prove nothing)
Two compensating width errors cancel in a size total and leave every offset between them wrong. So I did not stop at the size assert. Ghidra names each unrecovered field after its own hex offset, which is ~1000 free assertions. `oracle.py` walks each struct packing fields sequentially, and for every `field_<hex>` / `_pad<hex>` asserts computed_offset == the offset in the name. All 25 structs now pass both the anchor check and the asserted size.

That check found three places where Ghidra's emitted C does NOT match the binary. All three are fixed above:
1. CGameObject.object_type is 1 byte at 8, not `int`. Proof: `mov 0x8(%ecx),%al` at 0x4B17BE, 0x4B17C1, 0x4CC114. The `_pad9[3]` Ghidra emitted only makes sense if the field before it ends at 9.
2. CSWSCreatureStats.race is 2 bytes at 0xDC, not `int`. Proof: the next field is named field_de.
3. CGameEffect.type is 2 bytes at 8, not `int`. Proof: `movzwl 0x8(%ecx),%edx` at 0x503A70, cross-checked by four accessors that pin later offsets exactly: GetInteger reads +0x34, GetFloat reads +0x38, CopyStringFromList reads +0x48, GetObjectID reads +0x78. With Ghidra's `int` every one of those lands 2 bytes off.
If you regenerate from `data/` at some point, keep these three overrides or the structs silently break.

THE CExoArrayList HAZARD (the thing most likely to be got wrong)
CExoArrayList is `{void* data; int size; int capacity}`, 12 bytes. Slot order verified, not assumed: `CExoArrayList::operator[]` 0x437C40 is `mov eax,[ecx]; lea eax,[eax+i*sz]` so +0 is the data pointer; `Add` 0x4213E0 compares [this+4] against [this+8], grows by doubling (min 8) through Allocate, writes at index [this+4], then `incl 0x4(%esi)` -- so +4 is size and +8 is capacity. Ghidra's names are correct and not swapped.

Reading slot 0 of one of these as an int returns THE DATA POINTER, not a value. Ghidra hides them as opaque `unsigned char x[0xc]`. I enumerated all 34 twelve-byte blobs across these 25 structs and classified every one by disassembly. The ones that ARE CExoArrayList:
- CSWSObject: effects 0x124, looping_vis_fx 0x130, effect_targets 0x13C, expression_list 0x18C, matched_expression_strings 0x1A0
- CSWSCreature: field_324 0x324, field_330 0x330, effect_icons 0x8F4, perceptions 0x920
- CSWSCreatureStats: feats 0x0, feat_remaining_uses 0xC, bonus_feats 0x18, level_stats 0x28
- CSWCCreature: visibility_list 0x360
- CSWSArea: omen_events 0x294
- CSWSModule: object_lookup_table 0x130, limbo_creature_list 0x1DC
- CScriptEvent: int_params 0x4, float_params 0x10, string_params 0x1C, object_params 0x28  <-- this is the one the project already got wrong once. `*(int*)(ev+4)` is a pointer. The ints are at `*(int**)(ev+4)[0..*(int*)(ev+8)-1]`.
The twelve-byte blobs that are NOT lists: CSWSObject.position 0x90, .orientation 0x9C, .spell_target_position 0x1B0; CSWCObject.position 0x24, .orientation 0x30; CSWCCreature.moving_orientation 0x1C4, .stationary_orientation 0x1D0, .field_1DC; CSWSDoor.bounding_box_1 0x338, .bounding_box_2 0x344 -- all Vector (3 floats). And CSWSObject/CSWCObject/CSWSArea `game_object` is an embedded CGameObject.
Discriminator used: Vector shows `flds`/`fsubs` at base, base+4 and base+8; a list shows a dword load at base that is then dereferenced with base+4 as the loop bound. Two cases came out opposite to the name: CSWCCreature.field_1DC is a Vector (`flds 0x1dc/0x1e0/0x1e4` subtracted from position), and CSWSCreature.field_324 / field_330 are lists of u32 object ids.

SECOND, LESS OBVIOUS FORM OF THE SAME HAZARD
Ghidra sometimes splits a CExoArrayList into three separate scalar fields instead of one blob, so it does not look like a list at all. Two proven cases in CSWSArea: 0x190/0x194/0x198 (all object ids in the area -- CSWSArea::AddObjectToArea 0x50DFD0 loops `[ebx+0x194]` times over `[ebx+0x190]` with stride 4) and 0x1A0/0x1A4/0x1A8 (grown through CExoArrayList::Allocate 0x5E03C0). CItemRepository 12/16/20 is the same shape. This census is NOT complete -- I only proved the cases I hit. Detection recipe for the rest: in a class's own methods look for `cmp` of [this+N+4] against [this+N+8] followed by `test/je/add reg,reg` (the doubling), or a `lea 0xN(%this),%ecx` immediately before a call into the CExoArrayList method family; N is the data pointer. Attribution is unreliable when the base register came out of a call, so confirm each hit by eye.

HOW A SCRIPT GETS A POINTER TO A LIVE OBJECT (the chain that makes all of this usable)

1. `CAppManager** g_pAppManager = (CAppManager**)0x007A39FC`. One global, in .data. 5680 instructions reference it. The idiom throughout the image is `mov ecx,[0x7A39FC]; mov ecx,[ecx+8]`.
2. `CAppManager+8` is the `CServerExoApp*`. (`+4` is the `CClientExoApp*`.)
3. `CServerExoApp::GetGameObject` (0x4AE750) is two instructions: `mov ecx,[ecx+4]` (CServerExoApp+4 = CServerExoAppInternal*) then `jmp 0x4B1700`.
4. `CServerExoAppInternal::GetGameObject` (0x4B1700) does `mov ecx,[ecx+0x1005C]` -- that field is the `CGameObjectArray*` -- and calls 0x4D8230 with (id, &out). It then compares AL against the byte at 0x74666C, which is 0, so AL==0 means found.
5. `CGameObjectArray::GetGameObject` (0x4D8230) is a hash lookup, not a tree walk despite the field name. bucket = `((id>>31)&1)*0x1000 + (id & 0xFFF)` into an 8192-entry dword table at CGameObjectArray+0. Each chain node is 12 bytes `{u32 id_masked, void* object, node* next}`; it compares node[0] against `id & 0x7FFFFFFF` and follows node[8] on a miss. On hit it writes node[4] to the out-parameter and returns AL=0; on miss it writes NULL and returns AL=1. Return polarity is inverted from what you would guess.

Typed getters add one check on top. `CServerExoApp::GetCreatureByGameObjectID` (0x4AE770 -> internal 0x4B1790) does the lookup, compares the type byte at obj+8 against the constant at 0x746634 (= 5), then calls `vtable+0x30`. The type constants are all in .rdata and I read every one from the getter that uses it: area 4 (0x746633, getter 0x4B17E0), creature 5 (0x746634), item 6 (0x746635, getter 0x4B1740, vtable+0x38), trigger 7 (0x746636, getter 0x4B1880), placeable 9 (0x746638, getter 0x4B18D0, vtable+0x58), door 10 (0x746639, getter 0x4B1920, vtable+0x18), area-of-effect 11 (0x74663A, getter 0x4B1970, vtable+0x50), waypoint 12 (0x74663B, getter 0x4B19C0), encounter 13 (0x74663C, getter 0x4B1A10, vtable+0x5C), sound 16 (0x74663E, getter 0x4B1A60, vtable+0x68). There is one more getter (0x4B1AB0, vtable+0x64) matching type 14; I did not name it, so do not assume "store".

THE DOWNCAST IS FREE, AND I CHECKED
Those vtable slots are type-checked casts, not accessors. On the CSWSCreature vtable (0x7470C8) slot 0x30 points at 0x641DB0 = `mov eax,ecx; ret` and every other slot in the 0x28..0x5C block points at 0x63E7F0 = `xor eax,eax; ret`. On the CSWSDoor vtable (0x7498B0) the identity is at slot 0x18 instead, and 0x30 is the null stub. So: once the type byte matches, the subclass pointer is bit-identical to the CGameObject* -- no adjustment. A runtime may check `obj->object_type` itself and cast directly, and does not have to make the virtual call. CSWSItem is the exception to watch: its embedded CSWSObject starts at +16, so `item+16` is the CSWSObject and `item+16` is where the CGameObject header lives.

CLIENT SIDE
The cheap path is the cross-link, not a second traversal: CSWSObject+548 holds the `CSWCObject*` (read and cached by CSWSObject::GetClientObject 0x4CC2B0) and CSWCObject+248 holds the `CSWSObject*` back (CSWCObject::GetServerObject 0x63D4B0). Both offsets verified by disassembling those two accessors. The independent path is `CAppManager+4` -> CClientExoApp -> GetGameObject 0x5ED580 / GetCreatureByGameObjectID 0x5ED5B0 / GetGameObjectArray 0x5ED570.

TWO SMALL CAVEATS
`CScriptVarTable` is a name I coined for the recurring 20-byte script-variable blob (CSWSObject+272, CSWSArea+500, CSWSModule+156). There is no type by that name in the corpus, so do not send a generator looking for one.
The 8-byte string blobs are split between CExoString `{char*, u32 len}` and CExoLocString `{void*, i32 strref}` -- both are 8 bytes, so size cannot tell them apart. I used the field name (anything with loc/localized reads as CExoLocString) and marked all of them `med`. Verify per field before a script exposes one as text.
